title: Entering the room
hook: Balaam's words "how goodly are thy tents" are said on entering a synagogue

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev, the service of the heart. Your line was prayer is the heart's work. Today, the words many people say at the synagogue door.

Doorways change people. You lower your voice walking into a library. You straighten your back at a job interview. At some homes you take your shoes off before anyone asks. A threshold is a small border. In many synagogues, the first words people say on entering come from a surprising source: a foreign prophet who had been hired to curse.
screen: `QUIET IN THE LIBRARY.` → `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `WORDS FROM A HIRED PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Back in Numbers, King Balak of Moab hires the prophet Balaam to curse Israel. Balaam climbs a height, looks down at the camp spread across the valley, tribe by tribe, and blessing comes out of his mouth instead: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob, Thy dwellings, O Israel!" In Hebrew, mah tovu: how good. What did he see? The Talmud, in Bava Batra, and Rashi after it, point to a detail. The tents were set up so that no doorway faced another. Each family had its privacy: a huge camp, and no one peering into anyone else's home. The respect was visible from the hilltop. The rabbis read tents and dwellings as houses of prayer and houses of study, so the verse became words for entering a synagogue. In many siddurim, mah tovu stands at the very beginning of the morning prayers, followed by a psalm verse about coming into God's house through God's great kindness. And there's a twist. These are an outsider's words, someone sent to do harm, who looked closely and saw goodness. A few later teachers were uneasy about opening prayer with Balaam's words. The custom stayed. Some find it moving that, in many prayer books, the morning begins with what a stranger saw: a community that respects one another's doors.
screen: `BALAAM, HIRED TO CURSE.` · `MAH TOVU: HOW GOOD.` · `NO DOOR FACING ANOTHER.` · `AN OUTSIDER'S WORDS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `HOW GOOD THESE TENTS.`

segments.voice: Picture the next doorway you'll walk through, a home, a classroom, an office, a place of worship, and see yourself stopping just before it for a single breath. If you pray, mah tovu is there: how goodly are thy tents, O Jacob. If not, notice what's good about the place you're about to enter, and the people inside.
Mah tovu. How good — Balaam's blessing on seeing Israel's tents, each respecting the other's doorway, said now on entering a synagogue.
Your line: how good these tents. A stranger came to curse, looked closely, and saw goodness. That's day five hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Many Jews say mah tovu (Numbers 24:5) on entering a synagogue in the morning, followed by verses from the Psalms; in many siddurim it is the first passage of the morning service.

chat.says: Why do some synagogues greet you with Balaam's words? Wasn't he hired to curse Israel?
options: Yes, but he looked down, saw no door facing another, and blessed them instead.
They're really Moses' words; Balaam only repeated them after hearing Israel pray.
Balaam later joined Israel, and these were the words he spoke when he arrived.
chat.meaning: In Numbers, Balaam came to curse but blessed Israel's tents; the Talmud says no doorway faced another, so the rabbis made it words for entering.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'Many find it moving that the prayer book begins' softened to 'some readers... in many prayer books', since placement varies by rite.
Numbers 24:5 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Bava Batra 60a: Balaam saw that the openings of their tents did not face each other; Rashi on Numbers 24:2/24:5. Sanhedrin 105b: tents and dwellings as synagogues and study houses. Paraphrased.
Objection to opening with Balaam's words is associated with the Maharshal (16th century); kept as 'a few later teachers'.
Placement of mah tovu at the start of the morning service varies by rite (common in Ashkenazi siddurim).
Balaam was covered in Block C (Balak); the review of this day refers back to it lightly.
